content:
Hi! I started learning theorem proving few weeks ago in Lean and found it very enjoyable. If I had plenty of time, I could spend forever just turning real-world proofs in papers and textbooks into Lean.

However, I also observe the recent growth of LLM's proving skills. I know there is an LLM dedicated for formal proving, and saw a recently-proved Erdős Problem formalized in just a few days, or even a report that an entire textbook was successfully turned into Lean.

Given these situations, I am wondering, as a beginner who doesn't really understand the current status of the community, what work is left to human? I am feeling like if we can consume tokens as much as we want, we may let AIs prove any theorems we want, so the only tasks left to human is choosing what to let them work on, or building a better architecture on automated proving.

Of course I know that is not always the case. On one hand I also see Fermat's Last Theorem is not proved (automatically), which implies that LLMs cannot handle cutting-edge mathematical concepts. On the other hand I also see a conversation in this Zulip chat saying that an AI generated proof is not likely to be accepted in a specific repo, maybe in Mathlib.

This implies that AIs do still lack some abilities; what do you think it is?
I feel like this also give me an idea of what kind of contribution I can do to this community in the future.

I just posted an example of a challenge which humans did nearly 200 years ago and which I think autoformalization tools will find difficult to do today, here #Autoformalization > Jacobian challenge @ 💬

The most difficult part of formalization is, and has always been, to write definitions. There are usually various ways of formalizing a mathematical definition, and they are correct in a certain sense. On the other hand, some of them make the formalization of theorems very painful, sometimes immediately, sometimes only when the math becomes more difficult. For these reason a mathematical library as mathlib needs to be designed in a very careful way: the goal is not only "write a sorry free proof of theorem X", but more importantly "make the formalization process as smooth as possible". LLM don't care much about "suffering", if they have to insert a chain of 5 canonical identifications in a proof they just do it, while a human would start thinking to "can I reformulate something and avoid this maps"? Of course you can try to ask the LLM to do so, but there is no evidence they are able to come up to genuinely new solutions. Note that these things really happen, we changed the definition of groups a couple of years ago since we suffering too much.
So the short answer is: in my opinion they are not good in making design choices, and those choices are fundamental in the design of a large library.

Thank you for your answers. I clearly understood from your opinions that what matters nowadays is designing the interface (definitions) rather than the contents (proofs). This is actually what I started to feel after I kind of get used to theorem proving itself; when I inspected "Undergrad math not in mathlib" list or "missing theorems from the 100 theorems," I found it more challenging to express the statement than writing the proof. As a programmer, this seems analogous to the different difficulties between writing an executable program and a library (API).

This viewpoint also matches the fact that formalizing elementary problems from IMO or entrance exams do not suffer so much from how to formalize the statement. But I also guess that this i s the field where AIs are in general good at, right? Even if I am capable of generating bunch of formalized version of hard but elementary math problems, that is nothing more than an exercise and a self satisfaction, and does not really contribute to the community, does it? If I want to step forward and do something fruitful to Lean development, maybe I should learn more about how to structure mathematical concepts in reusable ways?

T H said:

Even if I am capable of generating bunch of formalized version of hard but elementary math problems, that is nothing more than an exercise and a self satisfaction, and does not really contribute to the community, does it?

Doing such things can be a lot of fun and it contributes to you learning how to use the system. Formalizing is hard. My personal route was (read #tpil and prove lots of 1st year undergrad level theorems) [taught me the basics] -> (moderately complex definition) [taught me about typeclass inference] -> (quite difficult definition) [taught me a lot about library design] -> (actually start contributing useful content to Mathlib).
Learning to write proofs is in my opinion a very important prerequisite to learn how to write definitions/structure libraries.

If I had plenty of time, I could spend forever just turning real-world proofs in papers and textbooks into Lean.

I am in a similar boat, and personally I am using this good gamification energy to help me learn/relearn some areas of math. This is a separate question from how to contribute, but I find it very valuable personally. See https://rkirov.github.io/posts/lean6/ on how I use AI and lean to get me unstuck, but still being careful not to just automate myself out of the loop and fail my learning goals. Also see #general > self-learning math with lean @ 💬 for discussion on how to create the next set of leans companion, basically turning existing textbooks and exercises into lean puzzlebooks.

This implies that AIs do still lack some abilities; what do you think it is?

see #Autoformalization > questions of interest in autoformalization Not an AI person so can't speak to why that is, but roughly it is missing some sort of high-level lean design judgement when it has to build a new theory formally.
